title-group.article-title: Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors and Acute Kidney Injury Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials

sec.title: Rationale & Objective
sec.p: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) provide cardiovascular and renal benefits in individuals with or without type 2 diabetes. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the risks of acute kidney injury and other adverse events (AEs) associated with SGLT2is across diverse populations.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.title: Setting & Study Populations
sec.p: Thirteen RCTs comprising 84,581 participants were included. The studies encompassed diverse populations, varying in diabetes status, presence of chronic kidney disease, and SGLT2i dosages.

sec.title: Selection Criteria for Studies
sec.p: We included RCTs published through December 31, 2023, that evaluated the safety and efficacy of SGLT2is and reported renal and nonrenal adverse outcomes.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: Two reviewers independently extracted data and resolved discrepancies by consensus, focusing on renal and nonrenal AEs and subgroup analyses.

sec.title: Analytical Approach
sec.p: Random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled relative risks or odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: SGLT2is were associated with a 20% reduction in the risk of acute kidney injury (relative risk, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.74-0.87), with low between-study heterogeneity, supporting a consistent renoprotective effect. Among patients with chronic kidney disease, the risk of renal composite outcomes was also significantly reduced (odds ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.62-0.79). However, treatment was associated with increased risks of genital infections (P < 0.001), urinary tract infections (P = 0.03), diabetic ketoacidosis (P < 0.001), and hypovolemia (P = 0.008). No significant differences were observed for hypoglycemia (P = 0.08) or lower limb amputation (P = 0.07).

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Variability in study design, definitions of AEs, and patient baseline characteristics may influence the findings.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: SGLT2is conferred substantial renoprotective benefits but increases the risk of certain nonrenal AEs. Tailored treatment and close monitoring are crucial to ensure safety and efficacy, especially in high-risk patients.
Index Words: SGLT2 inhibitors, acute kidney injury, renal protection, kidney failure, chronic kidney disease

abstract.title: Plain-language Summary
abstract.p: Doctors are exploring new ways to protect the kidneys, especially in people at risk for acute kidney injury (AKI), a sudden loss of kidney function. Medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), first used to treat diabetes, have shown promise for kidney and heart protection. We reviewed data from major clinical trials to see if these drugs help lower the risk of AKI. Our findings showed that people who took SGLT2is were less likely to experience AKI, even if they did not have diabetes. However, some users experienced more side effects, like dehydration or infections. These results suggest that SGLT2is may help protect the kidneys when used carefully, particularly in people already at higher risk for kidney problems.

sec.p: Collection date 2026 Mar.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains a significant global health concern, contributing to substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs.1 Its prevalence continues to rise, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where healthcare resources are often limited.2 AKI, characterized by a rapid decline in renal function, not only increases short-term mortality but also predisposes patients to long-term complications, including chronic kidney disease (CKD), patients receiving kidney replacement therapy (KRT), and heightened cardiovascular risks.3, 4, 5, 6 Despite advancements in critical care and nephrology, the management of AKI remains largely supportive, focusing on fluid resuscitation, hemodynamic optimization, and the avoidance of nephrotoxic agents.1 Unfortunately, these measures have shown limited success in altering the disease trajectory.7,8 This emphasizes the pressing need for novel therapeutic interventions that can prevent AKI or mitigate its severity.9,10

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), originally developed as antidiabetic agents, have emerged as promising tools not only for glycemic control but also for cardiovascular and renal protection. By inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules, SGLT2is induce glycosuria and natriuresis, leading to downstream effects such as improved renal oxygenation, reduced oxidative stress, and decreased tubular workload. These mechanisms are thought to play a critical role in protecting against AKI.11 In addition, SGLT2is have demonstrated consistent benefits in reducing heart failure hospitalizations and slowing CKD progression across diverse populations.12,13

Preclinical studies suggest that SGLT2i may confer renoprotective effects by alleviating the workload on the proximal tubules, thus reducing tubular injury and inflammation.14 Additionally, SGLT2is appear to improve renal oxygenation and diminish oxidative stress, both of which play a critical role in AKI pathogenesis.15,16 Furthermore, observational data from patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and CKD indicate a lower incidence of dialysis dependence and mortality among SGLT2i users.17 However, despite these promising findings, robust evidence specifically evaluating the impact of SGLT2i on AKI risk reduction remains limited. Most clinical insights are derived from post hoc analyses of larger cardiovascular or renal outcome trials, leaving critical knowledge gaps regarding patient selection, dosage optimization, and subgroup-specific benefits.18,19

To address these gaps, this systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the efficacy of SGLT2is in reducing AKI risk and adverse renal outcomes across diverse patient populations. By doing so, this study aims to provide a clearer understanding of the therapeutic potential of SGLT2is in AKI prevention and guide evidence-based clinical decision-making.

sec.title: Protocol Registration
sec.p: This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols guidelines. The protocol was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews under registration number CRD42024599811.

Ethical approval was granted by the Kaohsiung Medical University Hospital Institutional Review Board under the exemption protocol number KMUHIRB-EXEMPT(II)-20250007. As this study involved secondary analysis of deidentified data from previously published RCTs, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.

sec.title: Search Strategy and Selection Criteria
sec.p: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across four major electronic databases: PubMed, EMBASE, Dynamed, and the Cochrane Library, covering studies published up to December 31, 2023. The search strategy incorporated medical subject headings and free-text terms, including keywords such as “Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors,” “SGLT2i,” “acute kidney injury,” and related phrases to identify meta-analyses that reported AKI as an adverse event (AE).

The search process was conducted in two phases: first, an initial search focused on identifying foundational RCTs reporting renal outcomes associated with SGLT2is, including landmark studies such as the EMPA-REG OUTCOME (Empagliflozin Cardiovascular Outcomes Event Trial in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients), the CANVAS (Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study), the DECLARE-TIMI 58 (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events), and the CREDENCE (Canagliflozin and Renal Events in Diabetes with Established Nephropathy Clinical Evaluation). Second, updated search (2019-2023): a secondary search was conducted to capture recently published RCTs using similar search terms like “Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors” and “Acute Kidney Injury.” We included all event-driven kidney outcome trials comparing SGLT2is with either an active or placebo control in patients, such as DAPA-CKD (Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Chronic Kidney Disease), DAPA-HF (Dapagliflozin in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction), EMPEROR-Reduced (Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients with Chronic Heart Failure and a Reduced Ejection Fraction), SOLOIST-WHF (Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Recent Worsening Heart Failure), and EMPA-KIDNEY (Empagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease). Additionally, the bibliographies of relevant meta-analyses and review articles were manually screened to ensure no eligible studies were overlooked. Unpublished data or conference abstracts were excluded unless they provided sufficient details for analysis.

The inclusion criteria are as follows: first, RCTs evaluating SGLT2is (eg, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, sotagliflozin, and ertugliflozin). Second, studies reporting AKI as a primary or secondary outcome. Third, studies including adult patients (≥18 years) across diverse clinical conditions (eg, diabetes status, CKD, and heart failure). The exclusion criteria are as follows: first, observational or retrospective studies. Second, trials without AKI-specific endpoints or insufficient data for statistical analysis. Third, studies focused exclusively on nonrenal AEs. Fourth, in the EMPA-REG trial, acute renal failure (ARF) events were reported under the broader category of renal AEs. Because ARF is an outdated term with limited current clinical relevance, these events were excluded from our meta-analysis of AKI (the complete search strategy and inclusion criteria are detailed in Fig 1 and Item S1).

caption.p: Flowchart of the study selection process. This figure illustrates the systematic process of identifying, screening, and selecting studies for inclusion in the meta-analysis. Reasons for exclusion at each stage are detailed within the methods.

sec.title: Data Extraction and Quality Assessment
sec.p: Two independent reviewers performed data extraction using a standardized data collection form. Key data points included, first, study design and population characteristics. Second, details of SGLT2i interventions (eg, drug name, dosage, and treatment duration). Third, definition and incidence of AKI and renal composite outcomes. Fourth, incidence of nonrenal AEs (eg, genital infections, urinary tract infections, hypovolemia, and diabetic ketoacidosis). Fifth, risk estimates (eg, relative risk [RRs], odds ratio [ORs]) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer when necessary.

sec.title: Outcome Definitions
sec.p: The primary outcome was the incidence of AKI, as defined and reported in each included trial. AKI definitions varied across studies and were based on the KDIGO 2012 criteria, used in trials such as EMPA-KIDNEY (eg, ≥ 1.5 × baseline within 7 days); study-specific definitions, such as doubling of serum creatinine or investigator-adjudicated AKI events (eg, DAPA-CKD, DAPA-HF, and CREDENCE); or Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities-coded preferred terms or standardized medical queries identifying AKI events or serious AEs requiring hospitalization.

Trials using outdated terms such as “acute renal failure” (eg, EMPA-REG OUTCOME) without sufficient clarity on threshold or timing were excluded from the AKI meta-analysis. When both laboratory and serious AE-based definitions were available, preference was given to adjudicated laboratory-based outcomes. Time windows (eg, 48 hours to 30 days) and thresholds were accepted if consistent with standard KDIGO or comparable frameworks. Details for each trial’s original AKI definition are provided in Table S1.

Nonrenal AEs included diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), genital infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), hypovolemia, hypoglycemia, and lower limb amputation. Definitions for all outcomes and AES are detailed in Table 1, Table 2, Table 3 and Table S2 to ensure transparency and reproducibility. The subgroup analyses were prespecified based on diabetes status (T2DM vs non-T2DM), presence of CKD, and SGLT2i dosage (standard vs low dose).

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: Data extraction was performed using the Cochrane RevMan Web tool. In cases where numerical data were not provided, we extracted values from figures within the publications. Wherever possible, we prioritized data on sustained kidney outcomes confirmed by repeat assessments, excluding transient fluctuations in kidney function or cases of dialysis initiation for AKI. In instances where only nonsustained outcomes were reported, these were included in the analysis as well.

sec.title: Search Results
sec.p: Our systematic search yielded 138 publications after applying our search strategy across PubMed, EMBASE, DynaMed, and the Cochrane Library. After eliminating 27 studies focused exclusively on nonrenal AEs, 111 investigations remained. We excluded an additional 20 studies with fewer than 1,000 participants and 67 findings that did not report AKI-specific outcomes or lacked sufficient data for analysis. Two studies focused on patients with type 1 diabetes were omitted to maintain a uniform population. Finally, eight active comparator trials were discarded, resulting in 13 RCTs with a total of 84,581 participants included in our meta-analysis (Fig 1).

sec.title: AKI in RCTs
sec.p: Across 13 RCTs involving 84,581 patients with an average follow-up of 3 years, 2,140 cases of AKI were reported. Among the 44,391 patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, 956 AKI events were recorded, compared with 1,184 serious AEs in the 42,935 control patients (Figure 2). For the primary outcome analysis, SGLT2is demonstrated a 20% reduction in AKI risk (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.74-0.87).

caption.p: Incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) events in patients treated with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors compared with placebo. This figure presents a comparison of the incidence of AKI events between patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors and those on placebo. The results are expressed as relative risk (RR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), indicating the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on AKI risk across the included studies.

sec.p: For the subgroup analysis, in patients with T2DM, SGLT2is were associated with a 25% reduction in AKI risk (RR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.69-0.82). In patients with non-T2DM, the risk reduction was less pronounced but still significant (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99). Trials like DAPA-CKD and EMPEROR-Preserved showed more pronounced benefits in populations with T2DM, whereas EMPA-KIDNEY highlighted significant benefits in patients with non-T2DM. In patients with pre-existing CKD, SGLT2is reduced AKI risk by 30% (RR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.62-0.79). In patients without CKD, the reduction was more modest (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.76-1.00). Trials such as CREDENCE and DAPA-CKD provided strong evidence supporting AKI risk reduction, specifically in populations with CKD.

For the dosage comparison, standard doses (eg, empagliflozin 25 mg and dapagliflozin 10 mg) significantly reduced AKI risk (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.72-0.85). Low-dose regimens showed a non-significant trend toward benefit (RR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.80-1.05).

sec.title: ARF in EMPA-REG
sec.p: In the EMPA-REG trial, which involved 7,020 patients with an average follow-up of 8 years, ARF events were reported as part of the renal AE category. Notably, ARF was an older term used to describe a syndrome characterized by an increase in serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels greater than 0.5 mg/dL and 10 mg/dL, respectively, as well as oliguria and changes in urine flow rate (Fig S1). Among the 4,687 patients treated with SGLT2is, 246 ARF events were recorded, compared with 155 events in the 2,333 control patients (OR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67-0.93; P = 0.004). No heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 0, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.84). Because of the outdated ARF terminology and its limited clinical relevance today, ARF events in EMPA-REG were excluded from the meta-analysis of AKI.

sec.title: Renal Composite AEs in Patients with CKD
sec.p: Three studies specifically reported AKI rates in patients with CKD, defined by an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) combined with albuminuria (Fig 3). Among 7,658 patients with CKD treated with SGLT2is, 382 AKI events were recorded, compared with 547 events in 7,656 control patients. A significant reduction of AKI was observed with the OR of 0.70 (95% CI, 0.62-0.79; P < 0.001). No heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 0, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.81).

caption.p: Renal composite adverse events in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) treated with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors compared with placebo. This figure presents the incidence of renal composite adverse events in patients with CKD who were treated with SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo. Results are expressed as relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), showing the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on the risk of composite renal outcomes in this subgroup.

sec.title: DKA-related AEs
sec.p: DKA-related AEs were reported in 13 studies involving 90,366 patients with an average follow-up of 3.2 years. Among 48,474 patients treated with SGLT2is, 121 DKA-related AEs were recorded, compared with 47 events in 41,892 control patients.

DKA-related AEs were significantly more frequent in patients treated with SGLT2is (OR, 2.11; 95% CI, 1.45-3.06; P < 0.001). Notably, the ORs indicated a significant increase in 4 trials (CREDENCE, DECLARE-TIMI 58, VERTIS-CV [Cardiovascular Outcomes with Ertugliflozin in Type 2 Diabetes], and SCORED [Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Chronic Kidney Disease]), whereas the other 9 trials showed no significant difference. Despite these variations, overall comparisons across trials revealed a statistically significant difference (P < 0.001), with low heterogeneity (I2 = 5%, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.4) (Fig 4A).

This figure presents the incidence of various nonrenal adverse events observed in patients treated with SGLT2is inhibitors compared with those receiving a placebo. Each panel illustrates the relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for a specific adverse event, highlighting the comparative safety profile of SGLT2is inhibitors. Each panel provides insight into the nonrenal safety profile of SGLT2is, supporting careful consideration of these risks in clinical practice.

sec.title: Hypoglycemia-Related AEs
sec.p: Hypoglycemia-related AEs were reported in 12 studies involving 80,301 patients with an average follow-up of 3.23 years. In total, 3,642 hypoglycemia-related AEs were reported among 42,757 patients treated with SGLT2is, compared with 3,772 events in 37,544 control patients.

No significant difference in hypoglycemia-related AEs was observed between the SGLT2is and control groups (OR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.93-1.00; P = 0.08). The DAPA-CKD trial showed a significant decrease (OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.26-0.95), whereas the other trials did not. No heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 0, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.72) (Fig 4B).

sec.title: Genital Infection-Related AEs
sec.p: Nine studies reported genital infection-related AEs involving 52,069 patients with an average follow-up of 3.16 years. Eight hundred seventy-eight genital infection-related AEs were recorded among 28,589 patients treated with SGLT2is, compared with 262 events in 23,480 control patients.

Genital infection-related AEs were significantly more common in patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors (OR, 3.33; 95% CI, 2.90-3.81; P < 0.001). Although DAPA-CKD, SOLOIST-WHF, and EMPA-KIDNEY did not show significant increases, an overall comparison revealed significant differences across trials (P < 0.001), with no heterogeneity detected (I2 = 0, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.94) (Fig 4C).

sec.title: UTI-Related AEs
sec.p: UTI-related AEs were reported in 11 studies involving 74,048 patients with an average follow-up of 3.32 years. Among 39,631 patients treated with SGLT2is, 2,976 UTI-related AEs were recorded, compared with 2,784 events in 34,417 control patients.

UTI-related AEs were significantly more common in patients treated with SGLT2is (OR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.13; P = 0.03). Significant increases were noted in VERTIS-CV (5 mg) and EMPEROR-Preserved, but other trials showed no significant difference. A comparison across trials revealed a statistically significant difference (P = 0.03), with low heterogeneity (I2 = 23%, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.21) (Fig 4D).

sec.title: Hypovolemia-related AEs
sec.p: Nine studies reported hypovolemia-related AEs involving 56,206 patients with an average follow-up of 3.34 years. Definitions of these AEs varied across studies. In total, 1,372 hypovolemia-related AEs were reported among 31,377 patients treated with SGLT2is, compared with 982 events in 24,829 control patients.

Hypovolemia-related AEs were significantly more frequent in the SGLT2i group (OR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.03-1.19; P = 0.008). However, individual trial ORs did not indicate a consistent increase. Overall comparisons revealed statistically significant differences across trials (P = 0.008), with no heterogeneity detected (I2 = 0, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.76) (Fig 4E).

sec.title: Lower Limb Amputation-Related AEs
sec.p: Lower limb amputation-related AEs were reported in 13 studies involving 90,338 patients with an average follow-up of 3.21 years. A total of 692 lower limb amputations were recorded among 48,449 patients treated with SGLT2i, compared with 518 events in 41,889 control patients.

Lower limb amputations did not differ significantly between SGLT2i-treated patients and controls (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.99-1.35; P = 0.07). Although the CANVAS trial indicated an increased risk, most trials did not. Low heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 29%, Cochran’s Q, P = 0.11) (Fig 4F).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 RCTs, encompassing 84,581 participants, provides robust evidence supporting the renoprotective effects of SGLT2is in reducing the risk of AKI. The trials assessed a range of SGLT2is—dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, and sotagliflozin—across diverse patient populations and clinical settings.

Our findings demonstrated a significant reduction in AKI risk with the use of SGLT2is, as reflected by a pooled RR of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.74-0.87), indicating a 20% reduction in AKI incidence with consistent results across diverse patient populations, including those with and without type 2 diabetes and CKD. This supports the role of SGLT2i not only in glycemic control but also in renal protection. Notably, trials such as DECLARE-TIMI 58,20 EMPA-REG OUTCOME,12 and EMPEROR-Preserved in diabetic patients,21 and EMPA-KIDNEY in patients without diabetes23 demonstrated statistically significant reductions in AKI risk, with hazard ratios showing upper bounds of the 95% CI below 1, underscoring their potential for renal benefit.

One of the strengths of this meta-analysis is the lack of heterogeneity across the trials, which adds robustness to our findings. This consistency, observed across different trials and patient populations, strengthens the evidence that SGLT2is confers significant AKI risk reduction. The uniformity of the results is particularly remarkable, given that heterogeneity is often a challenge in meta-analyses of clinical trials.

sec.title: Mechanisms Underlying Renoprotective Effects of SGLT2is
sec.p: The mechanisms underlying the protective effects of SGLT2is on the kidneys in the context of AKI are multifactorial. These agents reduce the level of glucose and sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubules, leading to glycosuria and natriuresis, which alleviates hyperfiltration stress on the glomeruli. This mechanism likely reduces the workload on the proximal tubule, mitigating tubular injury and inflammation.18 Additionally, SGLT2is improve renal oxygenation and reduce oxidative stress, which are critical contributors to the pathophysiology of AKI.16,23 The ability of SGLT2is to modulate inflammation and endothelial function may also play a role in these observed renal benefits.24 SGLT2is may attenuate renal inflammation and oxidative stress by modulating hypoxia-inducible factors 1α and suppressing proinflammatory cytokines.25 These effects collectively reduce tubular injury and apoptosis, thereby preventing the onset of AKI.

These findings have important clinical implications. AKI remains a common and serious complication, particularly in hospitalized patients, and is associated with increased mortality and health care costs. Current management of AKI is mainly supportive, emphasizing the need for novel therapeutic options. The renoprotective effects of SGLT2is, as demonstrated in this analysis, suggest that these agents could be integrated into treatment protocols for AKI, providing benefits beyond their established use in glycemic control and cardiovascular risk reduction.

sec.title: Subgroup Insights into SGLT2i for AKI Risk Reduction
sec.p: Our subgroup analysis revealed a more pronounced reduction in AKI risk among T2DM patients (RR, 0.75) compared with nondiabetic populations (RR, 0.88). This disparity might stem from the higher baseline risk of AKI in patients with diabetes because of chronic hyperglycemia-induced renal injury. Additionally, SGLT2is exert anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects, which may significantly impact diabetic populations where these pathways are more active. In patients with CKD, SGLT2is reduces AKI risk by 30% (RR, 0.70). The enhanced renoprotective effect in patients with CKD may result from a higher baseline tubular injury burden and increased susceptibility to ischemic injury. This finding reinforces the importance of SGLT2is as a therapeutic option in patients with CKD, regardless of diabetes status. Standard SGLT2i doses were associated with more significant AKI risk reduction (RR, 0.78) than lower doses (RR, 0.91). This observation suggests a dose-response relationship, highlighting the importance of optimal dosing strategies to maximize renal benefits.

Although SGLT2is demonstrated clear renoprotective benefits, our analysis also highlighted increased risks of specific nonrenal AEs, including DKA (OR, 2.11), genital infections (OR, 3.33), UTIs (OR, 1.07), and hypovolemia (OR, 1.11). These AEs warrant careful monitoring, particularly in high-risk subgroups such as elderly patients, those on concurrent diuretics, and those with baseline volume depletion. The risk of lower limb amputation did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.07), though the CANVAS trial reported a potential signal. This finding underscores the importance of individualized risk assessment before initiating SGLT2i therapy.

sec.title: Comparison with Previous Studies
sec.p: Our findings align with earlier meta-analyses and post hoc evaluations of cardiovascular and renal trials, such as DECLARE-TIMI 58, CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD, and EMPA-KIDNEY.22,26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31 However, this study goes further by incorporating a broader spectrum of patient subgroups and conducting detailed subgroup analyses, offering a more nuanced understanding of the renal benefits of SGLT2is.

The findings of this meta-analysis have important implications for clinical practice. First, broader use across patient populations: SGLT2is should be considered not only in diabetic populations but also in nondiabetic patients at high risk for AKI. Second, targeted monitoring and enhanced monitoring protocols for AEs such as DKA, genital infections, and hypovolemia should be implemented in clinical practice. Third, early intervention: early initiation of SGLT2i therapy in high-risk populations, such as patients undergoing cardiac surgery or intensive care admissions, may prevent AKI development.

However, several considerations must be acknowledged when interpreting these results. First, the included trials varied in their designs, patient populations, and the specific SGLT2i used, which may influence the generalizability of the findings. Second, the follow-up durations in these studies were relatively short, so the long-term renal outcomes and sustained effects of SGLT2is in AKI remain uncertain. Finally, questions regarding optimal dosing, timing, and patient selection for SGLT2i use in the context of AKI need further exploration.11

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has several limitations. First, although the trials included in the meta-analysis were large, multicenter RCTs, they varied in terms of study design, patient demographic characteristics, and definitions of renal outcomes. These differences could affect the generalizability of the findings. Second, the relatively short follow-up periods in the included trials limit our understanding of the long-term renal protective effects of SGLT2is. Third, while we focused on RCTs, observational studies and real-world evidence could provide additional insights into the broader applicability of these findings. Lastly, the optimal timing, dosage, and patient selection for SGLT2i use in the context of AKI prevention remain uncertain and warrant further research.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This meta-analysis confirms that SGLT2is significantly reduce AKI risk across diverse patient populations, with particularly strong effects observed in patients with T2DM, CKD, and those receiving standard dosing regimens. Despite an increased risk of nonrenal AEs, the overall benefit-risk profile strongly supports the use of SGLT2is as a preventive strategy for AKI. Clinicians should consider SGLT2is as a cornerstone therapy in high-risk populations while implementing monitoring strategies to mitigate potential adverse effects. Further research is warranted to optimize treatment protocols and clarify long-term renal outcomes.
